text: The Asia–Europe Meeting (ASEM) is a political dialogue forum designed to strengthen relations and promote various forms of cooperation between its partners. It was officially established on 1 March 1996 at the 1st ASEM Summit (ASEM1) in Bangkok, Thailand, by the then 15 Member States of the European Union (EU) and the European Commission, the then 7 Member States of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), and the individual countries of China, Japan, and South Korea. Over time, the forum expanded through a series of enlargements, including India, Mongolia, Pakistan, and the ASEAN Secretariat in 2008, Australia, New Zealand, and Russia in 2010, Bangladesh, Norway, and Switzerland in 2012, and Croatia and Kazakhstan in 2014. The ASEM Process is structured around three main pillars and is viewed by its partners as a means to deepen Asia–Europe relations at all levels to achieve a more balanced political and economic world order. This is supported by biennial meetings of Heads of State and Government, alternating between Asia and Europe, and biennial meetings of Foreign Ministers, along with other Ministerial Meetings and political, economic, and socio-cultural events at various levels. As of now, the ASEM Partnership comprises 53 Partners: 51 countries and 2 regional organizations. The countries include Australia, Austria, Bangladesh, Belgium, Brunei, Bulgaria, Cambodia, China, Croatia, Cyprus, the Czech Republic, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary, India, Indonesia, Ireland, Italy, Japan, Kazakhstan, Laos, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malaysia, Malta, Mongolia, Myanmar, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Norway, Pakistan, the Philippines, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Russia, Singapore, Slovakia, Slovenia, South Korea, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, Thailand, the United Kingdom, and Vietnam. The regional organizations involved are the European Union and the ASEAN Secretariat. Biennial Summits are held alternately in Asia and Europe and are attended by the Heads of State and Government of the respective partner countries and organizations. In addition, regular Ministerial Meetings are held on foreign affairs, financial, cultural, economic, educational, labor and employment, transport, or environmental issues, attended by the relevant ministers.
